result: In 30 human subjects, repeated presentations of visual gratings induced gamma-band activity in V1/V2 that decreased over the first ~10 repetitions and then increased over further repetitions. This pattern was stimulus-specific: when stimulus orientation changed at block boundaries, the biphasic pattern repeated. The gamma enhancement partially persisted when the same stimulus was repeated after 25 minutes of intervening stimuli with different orientations.
evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C29, C88-C90 collectively demonstrate the core finding with converging evidence from MEG recordings in 30 subjects. The biphasic gamma response (C4, C88), stimulus specificity (C5, C28, C45, C46, C89), and persistence over time (C6, C29, C92) are all supported by data from the experimental design with blocked stimulus presentations and statistical analyses controlling for confounds.

result: The repetition-related gamma changes were strongest in early visual cortex areas V1, V2, V3, and V4, as determined by source-localized MEG analysis.
evaluation: Claims C7, C40, C49 are supported by spatial analysis of source-localized MEG data shown in Figures 2e and 3e,f. The beamforming approach (LCMV and DICS) provided spatial localization of gamma responses to visual cortical areas, with all selected dipoles falling in V1 or V2 (C182).

result: Stimulus repetition increased gamma-band Granger causality, particularly in the feedforward direction from V1 to V2/V3/V4 and from V3/V3AB/V4 to higher visual areas. Feedback Granger causality to V1-V4 also increased, but feedforward increases were significantly stronger.
evaluation: Claims C8, C78-C82, C94 are supported by Granger causality analysis shown in Figure 5. The analysis used time-reversal testing to control for spurious connectivity (C85, C107-C108), and changes remained significant after controlling for gamma power changes (C85). The directional specificity and gamma-band clustering (C78-C79) provide converging evidence for repetition-related changes in functional connectivity.

result: Gamma peak frequency steadily increased over all repetitions of a given stimulus, without showing the distinct early decrease observed for gamma power.
evaluation: Claims C91 and C100 are supported by per-trial gamma frequency analysis shown in Figure 3b and statistical modeling (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b). The frequency increased by 0.05 Hz/repetition (p<2×10^-16) with no significant effect during the first 10 repetitions (p=0.19), contrasting with the biphasic pattern of gamma power.

result: The magnitude of early event-related field (ERF) components (C1 at 55-70 ms and C2 at 90-180 ms) steadily decreased with stimulus repetitions.
evaluation: Claims C95 and C101 are supported by ERF analysis shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c. Both C1 and C2 components showed stimulus-specific decreases during early repetitions (C1: p<5×10^-5, C2: p=0.03) and over further repetitions (C1: p=0.001, C2: p<2×10^-16), with effects persisting in block A2.

result: The repetition-related changes occurred over two timescales: gamma power and pupil constriction both decreased over the first 10 repetitions (with correlated slopes across subjects), but only gamma power increased over later repetitions while pupil constriction remained low. This pattern is consistent with superposition of an exponential decay (affecting both measures) and a slow increase (affecting only gamma).
evaluation: Claims C96-C99, C117-C119 are supported by pupil and gamma analyses shown in Figure 4. The correlation between gamma and pupil changes during early repetitions (r=0.45, p=0.013) but not later repetitions (p=0.20) supports the two-process interpretation. Time constant estimates (gamma: 3.5 repetitions, pupil: 5.6 repetitions) further support the exponential decay component.

result: The strong gamma response on the first trial of each block, followed by rapid decrease, is consistent with responses to unexpected and novel stimuli. Subjects were not informed about stimulus orientations or block structure, making stimulus switches unexpected, and grating stimuli were novel as they were not shown during training.
evaluation: Claims C109-C114, C119 provide a coherent interpretation of the early gamma decrease. The experimental design ensured stimulus novelty and unexpectedness (C110-C111), and prior research (C112-C114) supports stronger responses to unexpected/novel stimuli in early visual cortex. The correlation between gamma and pupil changes during early repetitions (C97, C118) further supports this interpretation.

result: Changes in gamma power were not driven by changes in microsaccade rate.
evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by control analyses showing that microsaccade rate did not change with stimulus repetition (p=0.66) and was not significantly associated with gamma power (p=0.17) in the regression model. This rules out microsaccades as a confound for the gamma findings.

result: Changes in reaction times and accuracy were not correlated with changes in gamma power across subjects.
evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by correlation analyses (all p>0.22) between per-subject changes in gamma power and behavioral measures. This indicates that the gamma changes were not directly reflected in task performance, consistent with the idea that synchronization compensates for reduced firing rates.

result: The study demonstrates remarkable similarities between gamma-band activities and repetition-related changes in humans (30 subjects) and non-human primates (2-4 subjects in prior studies), with the human study allowing population-level inference.
evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by comparison with the companion paper (Peter et al., 2020) and prior macaque studies. The large sample size (30 subjects) is a clear strength allowing population inference, though the claim of 'remarkable similarities' relies partly on the companion paper rather than direct comparison in this manuscript.

result: The authors propose a mechanistic model in which repetition-related gamma enhancement results from interaction between gamma cycle dynamics and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). In this model, strongly driven excitatory neurons (Estrong) spike early in the gamma cycle, followed by inhibitory neurons (Ilocal), then weakly driven neurons (Eweak). Hebbian STDP would strengthen Estrong-to-Ilocal and Ilocal-to-Eweak synapses while weakening Eweak-to-Ilocal and Ilocal-to-Estrong synapses, leading to increased gamma power/frequency, enhanced feedforward communication, and maintained performance despite reduced overall firing rates.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C137-C163 present a detailed mechanistic model that is theoretically plausible and consistent with the observed data (C153-C154, C159-C160, C163). However, this remains speculative (C10, C148, C150-C157) as the study did not directly measure spike timing, synaptic weights, or cell-type-specific responses. The model draws on established principles (STDP, gamma cycle dynamics) from prior work (C137-C147) but requires direct experimental validation.

result: The study acknowledges methodological limitations: MEG source localization has spatial resolution of 0.45-7 mm with careful head stabilization, and Granger causality indicates predictability rather than true neuronal interactions, with potential spurious connectivity from common noise/field spread that can be alleviated by time-reversal testing.
evaluation: Claims C105-C108 appropriately acknowledge methodological limitations and controls. The spatial resolution estimate (C105) is supported by citation, and the Granger causality caveats (C106-C108) are standard in the field. The use of time-reversal testing (C108) addresses a key concern about spurious connectivity.

result: Grating stimuli produced robust gamma-band responses in V1/V2 dipoles, with stimulus-driven decreases in alpha/beta power in temporal/parietal and parietal/frontal areas. The repetition-related increase was specific to the gamma band and to the stimulus period (not baseline).
evaluation: Claims C38-C39, C41, C50, C181-C182 describe basic stimulus-evoked responses that serve as validation of the experimental approach. The gamma responses were successfully localized to V1/V2 (C182), showed expected spectral specificity (C50), and were distinct from baseline activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).

result: The study included 30 participants (20 male, mean age 22 years) who completed a change detection task with grating stimuli presented in 5 blocks of 120 trials each. MEG data were recorded with 275 axial gradiometers, with careful control of head movement, eye blinks, and artifacts, resulting in 76% of trials being usable for analysis.
evaluation: Claims C164-C180 describe the methods and sample characteristics. The sample size (30 subjects) is adequate for population inference (C104), though gender imbalance (67% male) is noted. The data quality measures (3.9% blink rate, 76% usable trials, 9 excluded subjects) indicate rigorous quality control. Ethical approval was obtained (C167).
